item.title: Can you grow mushrooms from store-bought mushrooms?
item.description: Oysters often clone from fresh stem butts onto cardboard or agar. Grocery button and cremini rarely succeed. Methods, odds, and why results vary.
item.content:encoded:
Yes for oysters, rarely for grocery button or cremini. Fresh oyster (Pleurotus) stem butts often grow onto damp cardboard or sterile agar, and University of Florida extension even recommends starting a mother culture from market oysters. Grain spawn from that culture colonizes in about 10 to 20 days at 23 °C (73 °F). Button, cremini and portobello are Agaricus bisporus. They need Phase I and Phase II compost plus a casing layer, and U.S. grocery packs are mostly commercial hybrids that have already spent days in the cold chain. Cloning them at home almost never turns into a crop.

Short answer

You can clone some grocery mushrooms. You cannot plant a mushroom like a seed and expect a new cluster. What works is living mycelium still inside fresh tissue. Tear or cut that tissue onto a food source it can colonize, then grow it out into spawn and a fruiting substrate.

Pearl oyster (Pleurotus ostreatus) is the species that makes this practical at home. Cornell Small Farms lists oysters among the easiest edible mushrooms to grow and notes they run on straw, sawdust, shredded paper, coffee grounds and similar plant waste. Button / cremini (Agaricus bisporus) is a different story. Our profile tags it advanced and compost-only, and commercial California production still runs Phase I fermentation, a 10 to 14 day Phase II pasteurization and conditioning cycle, then casing before pins form.

Which store mushrooms clone

Grocery mushroomSpeciesStem butt on cardboardTissue on agarLikely home crop
Pearl, blue, pink, yellow oysterPleurotus spp.Often works with fresh buttsUF/IFAS standard methodGood on straw, cardboard or coffee mixes
King oysterPleurotus eryngiiSometimesYes with sterile techniqueNeeds woodier mix than pearl
Button, cremini, portobelloAgaricus bisporusRarelyPossible in a lab, hard at homeNeeds Phase II compost and casing
ShiitakeLentinula edodesPoorPossiblePrefers hardwood sawdust or logs

UF/IFAS (SS663) says oyster mushrooms can be cloned from the basidiocarp onto agar, and for isolation it recommends market oysters so you start with an edible cultivated strain. Stamets describes stem butts in Mycelium Running as a low-tech clone: many saprophytes with living basal mycelium will regrow when the butt is pressed into damp cardboard or wood chips.

Buttons fail for substrate reasons more than cloning theater. UC ANR notes that U.S. production is dominated by Agaricus hybrids grown as secondary decomposers on composted materials, not on raw straw. Ammonia left after Phase I is inhibitory and lethal to mushroom growth until Phase II removes it. Even a clean tissue culture has nowhere useful to go without that compost and a non-nutritive casing on top.

Tissue cloning vs stem butt on cardboard

Two common methods do different jobs.

Tissue on agar is the clean route. UF/IFAS: pull the oyster cap apart to expose the inside uncontaminated tissue, then move tiny pieces with sterile tweezers onto potato dextrose agar or a similar medium, ideally in a still-air box or flow hood. When white hyphae grow out without mold or bacteria, subculture the leading edge. That mother culture inoculates sterilized grain. Incubate at 23 °C (73 °F) in the dark until the grain is white, about 10 to 20 days. Store finished spawn at 4 °C (39 °F) for non-tropical Pleurotus strains, and subculture mother plates every 6 to 12 months.

Stem butt on cardboard skips sterile media. You use the dense base of the stem, where white fuzz (mycelium) often still shows, as the inoculum, and boiled corrugated cardboard as a low-nutrient first food. Cellulose-heavy cardboard favors aggressive wood and straw eaters like oysters and gives molds less to live on than rich grain. It is less reliable than agar, and yields from cardboard spawn are lower than from grain, but it needs no pressure cooker.

Use tissue cloning when you want a stable culture and grain spawn. Use stem butts when you want a cheap first try from tonight's oysters.

Stem butt cloning onto cardboard

  1. Pick the freshest oyster cluster you can find at the store. Caps should be firm, not slimy or darkened. Stamets stresses fresh tissue for any clone. Work the same day, or keep the pack refrigerated and use it within about two days.
  2. Tear plain brown corrugated cardboard into pieces that fit a clean plastic container. Avoid heavy ink where you can. Cover the pieces with boiling water, lid on, and let them cool to room temperature. Drain until a squeeze leaves them damp, not dripping.
  3. Melt a few small air holes in the lid with a heated nail. Wash your hands and wipe the work surface.
  4. Eat the caps. Tear (do not slice) the stem bases where the cluster was joined. Keep any white fuzz on the butts. Tearing exposes clean inner cells instead of dragging surface contaminants through the tissue the way a knife can.
  5. Lay a layer of damp cardboard in the container, spread the stem butts in one even layer, then cover with more cardboard. Pack enough butts that mycelium has a chance to meet and outcompete whatever else is on the board.
  6. Close the lid and keep the container dark at about 20 to 24 °C (68 to 75 °F). Check after about 10 to 14 days, and allow up to about 3 weeks before judging it.
  7. Success is white, thread-like mycelium running from the butts across the cardboard until the pieces bind together and smell earthy. Failure is green, black, orange or slimy patches, or a sour smell. Contaminated cardboard spawn is not salvageable. Throw the whole container out and start over with fresher mushrooms.

When the cardboard is mostly white, break it up into pasteurized straw, more boiled cardboard, or a fresh coffee-and-straw mix. Our coffee grounds guide and oyster kit day-by-day cover the next stages. Plan dates with the grow timeline calculator.

Why grocery mushrooms often fail

Age and the cold chain. Mycelium in a stem butt is living tissue. Days on a truck and under a misted case leave less vigor than a cluster picked that morning. Older packs get soft, wet and colonized by bacteria before you open them.

Species biology. Oysters are primary decomposers that run on pasteurized plant waste. Buttons are secondary decomposers that expect a finished compost. Cornell's urban mushroom sheet puts oysters on coffee grounds, straw and shredded paper. It does not put Agaricus there. Our button / cremini profile needs a spawn run of about 16 days on compost, then casing and pinning for about 8 days, then fruiting for about 12 days, with little to no light. Our pearl oyster profile colonizes about 14 days at 24 °C (75 °F), pins about 5 days at 18 °C (64 °F), and fruits about 10 days at 16 °C (61 °F) with blue light and heavy fresh air.

Cultivar and handling. UC ANR reports that Agaricus hybrids dominate U.S. commercial production, with white, off-white, cream and brown lines selected for farm rooms, not for cardboard buckets. Grocery oysters are usually vigorous cultivated Pleurotus strains, which is why UF/IFAS is comfortable starting a mother culture from a market pack.

Contamination. Cardboard and coffee methods are not sterile. Green mold (Trichoderma) and bacteria win when the butts are old, the cardboard is too wet, or the oyster share is too thin. See the contamination guide for what those failures look like.

Honest odds

Expect oysters to be worth trying and buttons not to be. With a firm, same-day oyster cluster, stem butt cardboard often colonizes; tissue on agar is more consistent if you can keep the plate clean. Either way you still need a pasteurized fruiting substrate and the humidity, fresh air and light in the oyster profile. A limp week-old pack is a kitchen experiment that usually molds.

For button, cremini or portobello from the store, treat success as unlikely. Even a clean agar plate needs Phase II compost free of ammonia, a casing layer, and cool humid pinning. That is farm infrastructure, not a windowsill project. If you want those mushrooms at home, get spawn and ready compost made for Agaricus, or start with oysters instead. Our easiest mushrooms guide and the grow at home pillar map the beginner path, and the grow hub links profiles and tools.

FAQ

Can you grow mushrooms from store-bought mushrooms?

Yes for fresh oysters, by cloning stem butts or inner tissue, not by planting the mushroom whole. Grocery button and cremini almost never become a home crop because they need compost and casing.

Do you need agar to clone oyster mushrooms?

No. Agar gives a cleaner mother culture and better grain spawn. Stem butts on boiled cardboard are the no-lab path Stamets describes for saprophytes with living basal mycelium.

How long does cardboard spawn take?

Check around 10 to 14 days and allow up to about 3 weeks. White mycelium binding the cardboard is success. Colored mold or a sour smell means discard it.

Why won't grocery button mushrooms grow on cardboard or coffee grounds?

Agaricus bisporus is a secondary decomposer. Commercial production uses Phase I and a 10 to 14 day Phase II compost cycle, then a casing layer to force pins. Cardboard and coffee suit primary decomposers like oysters.

Are grocery oyster mushrooms safe to clone?

UF/IFAS recommends cultivated market oysters for mother culture isolation so you start with a known edible Pleurotus strain. Still verify you bought cultivated oysters, not a wild lookalike, and discard any culture that grows mold.

Is cloning the same as growing from spores?

No. A tissue or stem butt clone keeps the genetics of that mushroom. Spores recombine and give new individuals. Cloning is how you copy a grocery oyster that already fruited well.

Sources

  • Liao, Hsu, Hameed and Cotter, Isolation of Mother Cultures and Preparation of Spawn for Oyster Mushroom Cultivation, UF/IFAS Extension SS663 / SL449
  • Liao, Hsu, Hameed and Cotter, D.I.Y. FunGuide: Grow Your Own Oyster Mushrooms at Home, UF/IFAS Extension SS662
  • Cornell Small Farms, Mushrooms (urban farming fact sheet)
  • de la Fuente and Davis, Commercial Production of Button Mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus) in California, UC ANR
  • Paul Stamets, Mycelium Running: How Mushrooms Can Help Save the World (Ten Speed Press), Chapter 9, Inoculation Methods: Spores, Spawn, and Stem Butts
  • Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms, 3rd ed. (Ten Speed Press), cited in UF/IFAS SS663 and in our profiles for chamber ranges
  • Our pearl oyster and button / cremini grow profiles, for stage lengths, temperatures, humidity, light and fan settings

item.title: Growing oyster mushrooms on coffee grounds
item.description: Coffee grounds grow oysters best as a quarter to a third of a straw or sawdust mix. What the trials found, how fresh grounds must be, and a bucket method.
item.content:encoded:
Use spent coffee grounds as part of the mix, not the whole thing. In a wheat straw trial, one part coffee to two parts straw by volume gave the best yield, at 105% biological efficiency. Two parts coffee to one part straw cut the yield in half, and coffee alone never fully colonized. In sawdust, fruiting stopped above about 30% coffee by weight in one study and at 50% in another, while a farm trial got good crops at up to 50% with baking soda added. Use grounds the day they are brewed, pasteurize the straw, and keep the coffee share at about a quarter to a third.

Can you grow oyster mushrooms on coffee grounds?

Yes, but not on coffee grounds alone. Oyster mushrooms are one of the easiest mushrooms to grow because they eat almost any plant waste, and University of Florida extension lists coffee grounds next to straw, corn cobs and paper as workable substrates. The catch is that spent grounds are a poor substrate by themselves. They are acidic, low in carbon compared to their nitrogen, and still carry caffeine. Mixed into straw or sawdust, they work well and can even raise the yield.

What the trials found

Four trials give a clear picture. The coffee share that works depends on what you mix it with and how you prepare it.

TrialBase substrateCoffee shareResult
Alsanad et al. 2021Wheat straw, pasteurized33% by volumeBest yield, 105% biological efficiency, about 815 g per bag
Alsanad et al. 2021Wheat straw, pasteurized67% by volumeYield and efficiency cut about in half, pins 6 days late
Alsanad et al. 2021None100%Never fully colonized
Chai et al. 2021SawdustOver 30% by weightFruiting inhibited
Carrasco 2018, commercial scaleSawdust25%Fruited
Carrasco 2018, commercial scaleSawdust50%Almost fully colonized, no mushrooms
SARE farm trialOak sawdust, sterilized, baking soda25 to 50%Reliable crops, 50% best with a second and often a third flush

Biological efficiency is the weight of fresh mushrooms divided by the dry weight of the substrate. At 105%, a kilogram of dry straw and coffee mix gave a little over a kilogram of fresh mushrooms.

The straw trial is the most useful one for a home grower. Wheat straw alone was the control. The one third coffee mix colonized only about a day slower than straw and pinned about 2.7 days later, then out yielded it. The two thirds coffee mix pinned 6 days late and gave about half the crop. Pure coffee, at pH 4.9 and a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 19 to 1, never finished colonizing.

The farm trial is the outlier at 50%, and it did a few things differently. It sterilized the mix instead of pasteurizing it, used oak sawdust, and added baking soda: 30 g for every 15 liter bucket of grounds and every 15 liter bucket of sawdust. Its bags averaged about 1 pound of fresh mushrooms per 6 pound bag of wet mix.

Why pure coffee grounds do not work

Caffeine and the nitrogen balance. In a University of Sydney study, caffeine held back oyster mycelium, and the more coffee in a coffee and sawdust mix, the slower the growth and the later or less likely the fruiting. The fungus broke down part of the caffeine as it grew. Pure grounds are also too rich in nitrogen. Straw sits around 69 to 1 carbon to nitrogen, and the one third coffee mix brought that down to 43 to 1, which the mycelium liked. Pure coffee at 19 to 1 was too far.

The grounds also add something useful. They bring the extra nitrogen that straw lacks, which is why a modest share beat straw alone.

How fresh do coffee grounds need to be?

Use them the same day they are brewed. Brewing at about 90 °C (194 °F) kills most of what is in the beans, so fresh grounds start out close to clean. A 2024 study of café grounds found bacteria below the detection limit and no fungi in grounds collected the same evening. Grounds picked up the next morning from a recycling facility carried over a million bacteria per gram. Two weeks of storage raised bacteria more than a hundredfold, and grounds stored open to air grew molds, including Aspergillus flavus.

Wet grounds at about 56% moisture are an easy meal for any mold, and that is your biggest risk. If you cannot use the grounds within a day, keep them in the freezer until you have enough, and pasteurize them with the straw instead of adding them raw.

Contamination risk with coffee grounds

The main threat is green mold, Trichoderma. The SARE farm lost bags to it early on and fixed it with better sterilization, draining excess water after sterilizing, cleaner hands and work area, and positive pressure airflow. Wet mix sitting at the bottom of a bag or bucket goes anaerobic and invites bacteria too.

What helps at home:

  • Use grounds within a day of brewing.
  • Keep coffee at a quarter to a third of the mix. A slow colonization gives molds a head start.
  • Drain the mix until no water comes out when you squeeze a handful.
  • Use plenty of spawn so the oyster mycelium takes over first.
  • Check weekly and throw out any bucket with green patches.

Our contamination guide shows what green mold, bacterial blotch and other common problems look like.

A small bucket method for coffee and straw

  1. Collect spent grounds the same day they are brewed, from your own coffee maker or a café. Pick out filters. Freeze them if you need a few days to collect enough.
  2. Cut wheat straw into 10 to 13 cm (4 to 5 inch) pieces and soak it overnight in water.
  3. Drain the straw and hold it in a hot water bath at 74 °C (165 °F) for 1 to 2 hours. A pillowcase or mesh bag keeps it under. Add any grounds older than a day to the bath in a fine mesh bag.
  4. Drain everything for about an hour and let it cool to room temperature. Work on a cleaned table from here on.
  5. Mix two parts straw with one part coffee grounds by volume. Then mix in oyster grain spawn at 5 to 10% of the substrate weight. More spawn colonizes faster.
  6. Drill 6 mm (1/4 inch) holes 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches) apart around a clean 5 gallon bucket. Pack the mix in firmly and close the lid.
  7. Keep the bucket dark at about 24 °C (75 °F). Check it weekly. Straw takes 2 to 3 weeks to go fully white, and coffee mixes can take a little longer.
  8. When the mix is white and pins start at the holes, move the bucket to cooler, damper air with light and fresh air. Pick when the caps flatten but the edges still curl under.

Use the substrate calculator to scale the straw, grounds and spawn to your bucket, and the grow timeline calculator to plan dates.

Fruiting settings for a coffee grounds bucket

Once colonized, a coffee and straw bucket fruits like any oyster block. These are the stage settings in our free pearl oyster grow profile.

StageDaysTemperatureHumidityLightFresh air
Colonization1424 °C (75 °F)90%DarkFan 15 s every 60 min
Pinning518 °C (64 °F)93%12 h a day, about 90 lux, blueFan 35 s every 15 min
Fruiting1016 °C (61 °F)88%12 h a day, about 90 lux, blueFan 40 s every 10 min

Oysters need a lot of fresh air. Too little gives long stems and small caps. Keep the surface just barely glistening, not dripping. Our oyster kit guide covers misting, light and harvest timing day by day.

FAQ

What is the best ratio of coffee grounds to straw for oyster mushrooms?

About one part coffee to two parts straw by volume. That mix gave the highest yield in a 2021 trial, at 105% biological efficiency. More coffee than straw cut the yield in half.

Can oyster mushrooms grow on 100% coffee grounds?

Not reliably. Pure spent grounds never fully colonized in the straw trial and are too acidic and too high in nitrogen. Mix them into straw or sawdust.

Do I need to pasteurize coffee grounds?

Not if they are used within a day of brewing. Fresh café grounds tested nearly free of microbes, while grounds collected the next morning from a recycling facility carried over a million bacteria per gram. Pasteurize older grounds with the straw.

Do mushrooms grown on coffee grounds contain caffeine?

Very little. The oyster mycelium breaks down part of the caffeine as it grows. The University of Sydney study estimated you would need to eat about 250 kg of fresh oysters grown on coffee grounds to get the caffeine in one espresso.

Why did my coffee grounds turn green?

That is almost always Trichoderma green mold. It grows fast on wet grounds that sat too long before use or a mix with too much coffee. Throw that batch out and start with fresher grounds and a lower coffee share.

Sources

  • Alsanad, Sassine, El Sebaaly and Abou Fayssal 2021, wheat straw and spent coffee ground substrates for oyster mushrooms, CyTA Journal of Food 19(1)
  • Carrasco-Cabrera, Bell and Kertesz 2019, Caffeine metabolism during cultivation of oyster mushroom with spent coffee grounds, Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology 103
  • Carrasco 2018, PhD thesis on oyster mushroom cultivation with spent coffee grounds, University of Sydney
  • Chai, Krishnan, Sabaratnam and Tan 2021, Assessment of coffee waste in formulation of substrate for oyster mushrooms, Future Foods 4
  • USDA SARE FNE17-874, Growing oyster mushrooms on spent coffee grounds and hardwood sawdust, final report
  • Hermansen et al. 2024, microbial load of spent coffee grounds during collection and storage, Applied Sciences 14(21)
  • Liao, Hsu, Hameed and Cotter, D.I.Y. FunGuide: Grow Your Own Oyster Mushrooms at Home, UF/IFAS Extension SS662
  • Our pearl oyster grow profile, for every stage length, temperature, humidity, light and fan setting above

item.title: Build an automated mushroom fruiting chamber with an ESP32 and ESPHome
item.description: Build an automated mushroom fruiting chamber with an ESP32 and ESPHome. Parts by role, wiring, an example YAML that runs a grow profile, and tuning.
item.content:encoded:
You need one ESP32 running ESPHome, a humidity sensor (an SHT40 or SHT41, plus an optional SCD41 for CO2), and three low voltage switches for a humidifier, a fan and an LED light. The firmware turns the humidifier on when humidity drops 1.5 points under target and off at 0.5 over, runs the fan for a set time on a set interval, and keeps the light on for a set number of hours. Our pearl oyster fruiting stage is 88% humidity, 40 seconds of fan every 10 minutes and 12 hours of light. The example YAML below runs that profile and shows up in Home Assistant.

What an automated fruiting chamber has to do

A fruiting chamber holds a colonized block and keeps three things where the mushroom wants them: humidity, fresh air and light. Temperature matters too, but most home builds handle it by putting the box in a room that is already close to the right temperature.

An ESP32 running ESPHome can do all of that for a few parts. It reads a sensor, switches loads, keeps working with no internet, and shows up in Home Assistant so you can watch graphs and change targets from your phone. It is the same approach our own firmware takes on the chambers we support, so the logic below is the logic we already run, cut down to fit one file.

If you own a Shrooly, you do not need to build anything. Install our free firmware on it instead. This post is for everyone else, and for anyone who wants a chamber that does not depend on one company staying in business. Our Shrooly alternatives page covers the other options.

Parts by role

Buy by role, not by brand. Any part that fills the role works.

RoleWhat to useNotes
ControllerESP32 dev board (esp32dev)Powered from 5 V
Humidity and temperatureSHT40, SHT41 or SHT45 breakoutI2C, address 0x44
CO2 (optional)SCD40 or SCD41 breakoutI2C, address 0x62
Humidifier5 V or 12 V ultrasonic mist maker, fogger or USB humidifierPick one that mists as soon as it gets power, with no button
Humidifier switchLogic level MOSFET module or a relay module that triggers at 3.3 VOne channel
Fan12 V PC case fanPulls room air in or pushes chamber air out
Fan switchLogic level MOSFET moduleLets the ESP32 set the speed
Light12 V LED strip, white or blueLow output is fine
Light switchLogic level MOSFET moduleOne channel
Power12 V supply plus a 5 V buck converterSize it for everything on at once
BoxClear tote or any sealed boxDrill holes for the fan and an exhaust

Keep every load on low voltage. If you want to run a mains heater or a mains humidifier, use a listed smart plug that Home Assistant can switch, not a relay board wired by hand.

The SHT4x is the better humidity sensor for this job. Sensirion rates the SHT40 and SHT41 at plus or minus 1.8% RH typical and the SHT45 at 1.0%. The SCD4x also reports humidity, but buy it for CO2. Its datasheet limits it to non condensing air from 0 to 95% RH, so keep it out of the mist.

Wiring

All three sensors share one I2C bus. Every load gets its own switch module. Tie every ground together: the 12 V supply, the buck converter, the ESP32 and each module.

PartConnects toESP32 pin
Sensor SDAI2C dataGPIO21
Sensor SCLI2C clockGPIO22
Sensor VCC and GND3.3 V and GND3V3, GND
Humidifier switch inputOn or offGPIO26
Fan MOSFET inputPWMGPIO25
Light MOSFET inputPWMGPIO27
ESP32 power5 V from the buck converter5V (VIN), GND

These pins were picked to stay clear of trouble. On the ESP32, GPIO0, 2, 5, 12 and 15 are strapping pins that change how the chip boots, GPIO6 to 11 usually connect to the flash chip, and GPIO34 to 39 are inputs only. Avoid all of those for loads.

Two things catch people out. Many relay modules switch on when the input goes low. If yours does, add inverted: true under the humidifier pin. And the SCD4x datasheet asks for a steady supply, with a separate regulator recommended, so do not hang it off a rail that also feeds the fogger.

Mount the sensor in the right place

Put the humidity sensor at the height of the block, out of the direct path of the mist and the fan. A sensor sitting in the fog stream reads 100% and turns the humidifier off while the rest of the box dries out.

High humidity is hard on these sensors. Sensirion says SHT4x parts build up a reversible upward offset, called creep, when they sit above about 90% RH for long periods, and that the built in heater clears it. Our firmware runs the heater in short pulses capped at 2% of the time, and the example below does the same. ESPHome does not publish readings while the heater runs, so a reading every 2 seconds still leaves plenty of data.

The example ESPHome YAML

This is an example to adapt, not a finished product build. It follows the same rules as our firmware, but it has not been tested on your parts. Check every pin and value against what you bought before you power anything.

What it does:

  • Turns every load off at boot. Nothing runs until you turn on the Auto mode switch.
  • Humidity: on below target minus 1.5 points, off above target plus 0.5, with at least 90 seconds on and 60 seconds off. Those are our firmware defaults. It shuts the humidifier off if the sensor stops reporting.
  • Fresh air: runs the fan for the set seconds every set minutes, and any time CO2 is over the limit or humidity is over 96%.
  • Light: on for the set hours starting at the set hour.
  • A Stage select that loads the colonization, pinning or fruiting stage of our pearl oyster profile. Every value is also its own number, so you can tune one without editing the file.
  • A button to calibrate the CO2 sensor to outdoor air. Delete the scd4x block and that button if you have no CO2 sensor.

Put your Wi-Fi details, an API encryption key and an OTA password in secrets.yaml next to it. ESPHome writes the key for you when you create a new device.

# Example to adapt, not a finished product build.
# One ESP32 runs a fruiting chamber from a grow profile:
# humidifier on/off with a band, fan on a fresh air timer plus a CO2 limit,
# light on a daily schedule. Pin numbers match the wiring table in the post.
# Check every value against your parts before you power anything.

esphome:
  name: fruiting-chamber
  friendly_name: Fruiting chamber
  on_boot:
    priority: 800
    then:
      # Every load starts off. The control loops turn things on.
      - switch.turn_off: humidifier
      - output.set_level:
          id: fan_pwm
          level: 0%
      - light.turn_off: grow_light

esp32:
  board: esp32dev
  framework:
    type: esp-idf

logger:

api:
  encryption:
    key: !secret api_key

ota:
  - platform: esphome
    password: !secret ota_password

wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password

time:
  - platform: sntp
    id: sntp_time
    timezone: America/Los_Angeles

i2c:
  sda: GPIO21
  scl: GPIO22

globals:
  - id: hum_changed_ms
    type: uint32_t
    initial_value: "0"
  - id: fan_cycle_start_ms
    type: uint32_t
    initial_value: "0"

sensor:
  - platform: sht4x
    address: 0x44
    update_interval: 2s
    # Short heater pulses fight the offset SHT4x sensors pick up above 90% RH.
    heater_max_duty: 0.02
    heater_power: Med
    heater_time: Short
    temperature:
      id: temperature
      name: Temperature
    humidity:
      id: humidity
      name: Humidity
      filters:
        - sliding_window_moving_average:
            window_size: 3
            send_every: 1

  # Optional. Delete this block if you have no SCD40 or SCD41.
  - platform: scd4x
    id: co2_sensor
    address: 0x62
    update_interval: 30s
    # ASC needs the sensor to see fresh outdoor air once a week.
    # A sealed chamber may never do that, so calibrate by hand instead.
    automatic_self_calibration: false
    co2:
      id: co2
      name: CO2

output:
  - platform: ledc
    id: fan_pwm
    pin: GPIO25
    frequency: 20000Hz
  - platform: ledc
    id: light_pwm
    pin: GPIO27
    frequency: 1000Hz

light:
  - platform: monochromatic
    id: grow_light
    name: Grow light
    output: light_pwm
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF

switch:
  - platform: gpio
    id: humidifier
    name: Humidifier
    pin: GPIO26
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF
  - platform: template
    id: auto_mode
    name: Auto mode
    optimistic: true
    restore_mode: RESTORE_DEFAULT_OFF

number:
  - platform: template
    id: target_humidity
    name: Target humidity
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    min_value: 60
    max_value: 96
    step: 1
    initial_value: 88
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: fan_every_min
    name: Fresh air every
    unit_of_measurement: min
    min_value: 1
    max_value: 240
    step: 1
    initial_value: 10
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: fan_run_s
    name: Fresh air run
    unit_of_measurement: s
    min_value: 5
    max_value: 900
    step: 5
    initial_value: 40
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: fan_speed
    name: Fan speed
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    min_value: 15
    max_value: 100
    step: 5
    initial_value: 45
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: co2_limit
    name: CO2 limit
    unit_of_measurement: ppm
    min_value: 500
    max_value: 2000
    step: 50
    initial_value: 800
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: lights_on_hour
    name: Lights on at
    min_value: 0
    max_value: 23
    step: 1
    initial_value: 8
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
  - platform: template
    id: light_hours
    name: Light hours
    unit_of_measurement: h
    min_value: 0
    max_value: 24
    step: 1
    initial_value: 12
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true

# Picking a stage loads that stage of the Pearl Oyster profile.
select:
  - platform: template
    id: stage
    name: Stage
    options:
      - Colonization
      - Pinning
      - Fruiting
    initial_option: Fruiting
    optimistic: true
    restore_value: true
    set_action:
      - if:
          condition:
            lambda: 'return x == "Colonization";'
          then:
            - number.set: {id: target_humidity, value: 90}
            - number.set: {id: fan_every_min, value: 60}
            - number.set: {id: fan_run_s, value: 15}
            - number.set: {id: fan_speed, value: 20}
            - number.set: {id: light_hours, value: 0}
      - if:
          condition:
            lambda: 'return x == "Pinning";'
          then:
            - number.set: {id: target_humidity, value: 93}
            - number.set: {id: fan_every_min, value: 15}
            - number.set: {id: fan_run_s, value: 35}
            - number.set: {id: fan_speed, value: 35}
            - number.set: {id: light_hours, value: 12}
      - if:
          condition:
            lambda: 'return x == "Fruiting";'
          then:
            - number.set: {id: target_humidity, value: 88}
            - number.set: {id: fan_every_min, value: 10}
            - number.set: {id: fan_run_s, value: 40}
            - number.set: {id: fan_speed, value: 45}
            - number.set: {id: light_hours, value: 12}

button:
  # Run outdoors for at least 3 minutes, then press. 426 ppm is the
  # NOAA global monthly mean for July 2026.
  - platform: template
    name: Calibrate CO2 to outdoor air
    on_press:
      - scd4x.perform_forced_calibration:
          id: co2_sensor
          value: 426

interval:
  # Humidity: on below target minus 1.5, off above target plus 0.5,
  # at least 90 s on and 60 s off. Same defaults as our firmware.
  - interval: 5s
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          const float rh = id(humidity).state;
          if (!id(auto_mode).state || isnan(rh) || rh <= 0.0f) {
            if (id(humidifier).state) id(humidifier).turn_off();
            return;
          }
          const uint32_t now = millis();
          const uint32_t held = now - id(hum_changed_ms);
          const float target = id(target_humidity).state;
          const bool on = id(humidifier).state;
          if (!on && rh < target - 1.5f && held >= 60000) {
            id(humidifier).turn_on();
            id(hum_changed_ms) = now;
          } else if (on && rh > target + 0.5f && held >= 90000) {
            id(humidifier).turn_off();
            id(hum_changed_ms) = now;
          }

  # Fresh air: run the fan for fan_run_s every fan_every_min minutes,
  # and any time CO2 is over the limit.
  - interval: 5s
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          if (!id(auto_mode).state) {
            id(fan_pwm).set_level(0.0f);
            return;
          }
          const uint32_t now = millis();
          const uint32_t every = (uint32_t) (id(fan_every_min).state * 60000.0f);
          const uint32_t run = (uint32_t) (id(fan_run_s).state * 1000.0f);
          if (now - id(fan_cycle_start_ms) >= every) id(fan_cycle_start_ms) = now;
          const bool scheduled = (now - id(fan_cycle_start_ms)) < run;
          const float ppm = id(co2).state;
          const bool co2_high = !isnan(ppm) && ppm > id(co2_limit).state;
          const bool too_wet = id(humidity).state > 96.0f;
          const float level = (scheduled || co2_high || too_wet) ? id(fan_speed).state / 100.0f : 0.0f;
          id(fan_pwm).set_level(level);

  # Light: on for light_hours starting at lights_on_hour.
  - interval: 30s
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          if (!id(auto_mode).state) return;
          const auto t = id(sntp_time).now();
          if (!t.is_valid()) return;
          const int start = (int) id(lights_on_hour).state;
          const int hours = (int) id(light_hours).state;
          const int since = (t.hour - start + 24) % 24;
          const bool want = hours > 0 && since < hours;
          if (want != id(grow_light).current_values.is_on()) {
            auto call = want ? id(grow_light).turn_on() : id(grow_light).turn_off();
            call.perform();
          }

Flash it once over USB with esphome run fruiting-chamber.yaml. After that ESPHome updates it over Wi-Fi. The lambdas use id(...).state, which is how ESPHome reads a sensor or number inside C++ code.

How to build the chamber, step by step

  1. Drill a fan hole low on one side of the box and an exhaust hole high on the other side, so fresh air sweeps across the block.
  2. Mount the humidifier so the mist goes into the open box, not straight onto the block or the sensor.
  3. Wire the sensor, the three MOSFET or relay modules and the power as in the wiring table, with all grounds tied together.
  4. Copy the example YAML, change pins to match your build, add secrets.yaml, and flash it over USB.
  5. Add the device in Home Assistant. It shows up on its own through the ESPHome integration.
  6. Run the box empty for a day with Auto mode on and watch the humidity graph.
  7. Tune the humidifier and fan until humidity holds near the target, then put the block in and pick the stage.

Run a grow profile

The Stage select loads these values from our pearl oyster profile. Change the stage on the day the profile says to.

StageDaysHumidityFresh airLightRoom temperature
Colonization1490%15 s every 60 min at 20%Dark24 °C (75 °F)
Pinning593%35 s every 15 min at 35%12 h from 8:0018 °C (64 °F)
Fruiting1088%40 s every 10 min at 45%12 h from 8:0016 °C (61 °F)

For another species, copy the values from its profile into the three if blocks. Our lion's mane profile wants damper air, for example: 94% to pin and 90% to fruit, with 25 seconds of fan every 18 minutes.

This build has no heater and no cooler. Our own firmware treats temperature the same way. It only controls temperature when Home Assistant switches an outside heater. Put the chamber somewhere that sits close to the stage temperature.

How to tune it

Humidity swings too far. If humidity runs well past the target before it drops, the mist maker is too strong for the box. Turn it down, move it away from the sensor, or raise the minimum off time. If humidity never reaches the target, the box leaks or the fan runs too long.

Check the sensor. Seal the sensor in a small jar with a damp paste of table salt. Saturated salt holds the air at about 75% RH at 25 °C. If your sensor reads far off that after a few hours, add an offset filter in the YAML.

Fresh air. Fresh air is a trade off. More of it keeps CO2 down but dries the box. The fresh air calculator turns your box size and fan into run times for a target number of air changes. University of California extension material suggests about 4 air changes an hour while oyster pins form and 4 to 6 while they crop. Our humidity and fresh air guide has the reasons.

CO2. With an SCD41 you can stop guessing. A SARE funded oyster guide says to keep CO2 under 800 ppm, which is the default limit in the example, and says oysters may not fruit above about 1,200 ppm. Long stems and small caps on oysters usually mean the box needs more fresh air.

CO2 calibration. The SCD4x automatic calibration assumes the sensor sees fresh air near 400 ppm for at least 3 minutes once a week. A closed chamber may never see that, so the example turns it off. Instead, take the sensor outside, let it run for at least 3 minutes, and press the calibrate button. The value in the YAML is 426 ppm, the NOAA global monthly mean for July 2026.

Home Assistant

The api block with an encryption key is what Home Assistant uses to talk to the ESP32. Home Assistant finds the device on your network and adds every sensor, switch, number and the Stage select as entities. From there you get history graphs, phone alerts if humidity drops, and a way to change stages without a laptop. The chamber keeps running its own loops if Home Assistant or Wi-Fi goes down.

Read our docs for how our firmware lays out the same controls on the chambers we support.

FAQ

What is the best sensor for a mushroom fruiting chamber?

An SHT40, SHT41 or SHT45 for humidity and temperature, mounted out of the mist. Add an SCD40 or SCD41 if you want to control fresh air by CO2. The SCD41 covers a wider range, 400 to 5,000 ppm against 400 to 2,000 ppm for the SCD40.

Do I need Home Assistant?

No. The ESP32 runs the humidity, fan and light loops by itself. Home Assistant adds graphs, alerts and an easy way to change settings.

Can I control a mains humidifier or heater?

Not with a hand wired relay board. Plug it into a listed smart plug and let Home Assistant switch it, or pick a 5 V or 12 V mist maker so everything in the box stays low voltage.

Why does my humidity sensor read 100% all the time?

It is in the mist path or it has condensation on it. Move it out of the fog stream. The SHT4x heater pulses in the example also help clear the high humidity offset.

Why turn off CO2 automatic calibration?

Automatic calibration assumes the sensor sees fresh outdoor air once a week. Inside a closed chamber that may never happen, and the sensor will drift. Calibrating by hand outdoors is more reliable.

Sources

  • Shroom Labs pearl oyster grow profile
  • Shroom Labs lion's mane grow profile
  • OpenShrooly firmware: humidity controls and defaults (controls.yaml)
  • OpenShrooly firmware: humidity control script
  • OpenShrooly firmware: SHT4x sensor settings (sensors.yaml)
  • Shroom Labs community ESPHome config for the Terrashroom
  • ESPHome SHT4X sensor
  • ESPHome SCD4X CO2 sensor
  • ESPHome native API
  • ESPHome template select
  • Home Assistant ESPHome integration
  • Espressif ESP32 GPIO reference
  • Sensirion SHT4x datasheet
  • Sensirion application note: creep mitigation for SHT4x
  • Sensirion SCD4x datasheet
  • Sensirion SCD4x sensor operation guide
  • NOAA global monthly mean CO2
  • Greenspan, Humidity fixed points of binary saturated aqueous solutions (NIST)
  • UC ANR, Growing oyster mushrooms
  • SARE and FungiAlly, Oyster mushroom cultivation guide

item.title: How to fruit a lion's mane grow kit
item.description: A lion's mane kit fruits in about 17 days once it is cut open. Day by day steps with humidity, fresh air, light, pink coloring and when to harvest.
item.content:encoded:
Cut one small X in a colonized kit, keep the air around it very damp, give it moderate fresh air and about 12 hours a day of low light, and keep it cool. Our lion's mane profile pins for 5 days at 18 °C (64 °F) and 94% humidity, then fruits for 12 days at 17 °C (63 °F) and 90%, under about 200 lux for 12 hours a day. That is about 17 days from opening to the end of the first harvest. Pick it while the spines are long and still white, before they turn yellow.

What a lion's mane kit needs to fruit

A lion's mane kit is a bag of hardwood substrate the mycelium has already grown through. To make it fruit you change four things: cooler air, very damp air at the cut, some fresh air, and a little light. Lion's mane is pickier than oyster on two of them. It wants the air damper, and it does better with less fresh air and less light than you might expect.

These are the settings in our free lion's mane grow profile. Pinning is when the first small knobs form. Fruiting is when they grow into a full head with hanging spines.

SettingColonizationPinningFruiting
Days16512
Temperature22 °C (72 °F)18 °C (64 °F)17 °C (63 °F)
Humidity90%94%90%
LightDark12 h a day, about 200 lux, blue12 h a day, about 200 lux, blue
Chamber fan15 s every 60 min25 s every 20 min25 s every 18 min

A kit arrives already colonized, so your count starts at pinning. Pinning plus fruiting is 17 days from cutting it open to the end of the first harvest. The whole profile, spawn to harvest, is 33 days.

Day by day steps for a lion's mane kit

  1. Day 0, check the bag. It should be mostly white and firm. Our profile colonizes at 22 °C (72 °F) in the dark, so a kit that still looks patchy can sit closed somewhere warm and dark for a few more days.
  2. Day 0, cut it open. Follow the instructions that came with the kit. If there are none, one small X on the side works. A 2025 lion's mane study cut a 3 by 3 cm X in each bag (Jozifek et al. 2025). Lion's mane grows from that opening, so one cut means one head.
  3. Day 0, move it somewhere cool and dim. Aim for around 16 to 20 °C (61 to 68 °F), with room light or indirect daylight, out of direct sun and away from heater vents.
  4. Days 1 to 5, keep the air very damp. This is the stage our profile runs wettest, at 94%. Mist the air around the cut and the inside of a loose tent a few times a day. Do not let water pool at the cut.
  5. Days 1 to 5, give it light and a little air. About 12 hours of low light a day and some fresh air tell the block it has reached open air. Look for dense white knobs at the cut, not a fuzzy white layer.
  6. Days 6 to 17, let the head grow. Keep the air damp, around 90%, and the room a degree cooler if you can, 17 °C (63 °F). Mist the air near the head, not the spines.
  7. By day 17, harvest. Cut the whole head off at the base once the spines have grown out, and before the tips turn yellow.
  8. After the harvest, rest and repeat. Clean up any bits left at the cut, let the block rest, then set it up the same way for a second flush.

Plug your open date into the grow timeline calculator to get calendar dates for each stage.

Why lion's mane wants high humidity

Dry air is the first thing to check with lion's mane. NCAT's ATTRA guide, a USDA funded grower program, aims for 85 to 95% humidity while fruiting and says lion's mane is especially sensitive to low humidity. When the air is too dry it forms small dense blobs instead of a full head with spines (NCAT ATTRA 2026). A review of lion's mane cultivation gives the same 85 to 95% range (Sokół et al. 2015), and the 2025 study grew it at 90 to 95% (Jozifek et al. 2025).

Wet is not the same as damp. NCAT links yellow or slimy spots and constant dripping to too much moisture or too little airflow. Mist the air, not the mushroom, and if water runs down the bag, ease off. A loose plastic tent with a few holes over the kit holds humidity between mistings in a dry room. Humidity and fresh air covers how the two trade off.

How much fresh air does a lion's mane kit need?

Some, but less than oyster. Our lion's mane profile runs the fan 25 seconds every 18 to 20 minutes while pinning and fruiting. Our oyster profiles run it 40 seconds every 10 minutes. The profile note is that too much air yellows the spines, and if the spines brown or yellow, cut fresh air and raise humidity a little.

Too little air causes a different problem. NCAT says that with low air exchange lion's mane turns fuzzy and misshapen (NCAT ATTRA 2026). The 2025 study vented its grow box to keep carbon dioxide under 800 ppm (Jozifek et al. 2025). A kit on an open counter usually gets enough. A kit in a closed cupboard or sealed bag does not.

Why lion's mane wants low light

Lion's mane needs light as a signal, not for energy, and it does not need much. The cultivation review gives 200 to 400 lux for fruiting (Sokół et al. 2015). Our profile runs about 200 lux for 12 hours a day and keeps colonization dark so the block does not pin early. Room light or a window with no direct sun is enough. Do mushrooms need light? has the numbers for other species.

More light is not better here, and that is where the pink comes in.

Why is my lion's mane turning pink?

Some lion's mane turns pink while it is young. The 2025 study from the Czech University of Life Sciences grew four strains. One stayed pure white in every trial. The other three showed pink in early development that got stronger with more selenium in the substrate and faded a bit as the heads matured (Jozifek et al. 2025). An earlier study also saw lion's mane go from white to white pink when selenium salts were added at 0.4 and 0.6 mM (Niedzielski et al. 2014).

A kit has no added selenium, so the part that matters at home is light. The 2025 study saw slight pink even in its plain controls, grown at 17 to 18 °C under about 500 lux for 24 hours a day. The authors point to the cool temperature, bright light and nonstop light as possible causes. When they dropped to 200 lux or lower on a 12 hour cycle, the heads came out white. They also call the pink a possible stress reaction and say it depends on the strain.

That is why our profile runs 12 hours at about 200 lux. If your kit is turning pink, shorten the light to 12 hours a day, move it away from bright light, and keep it in the 16 to 20 °C (61 to 68 °F) range NCAT gives for fruiting.

When to harvest lion's mane

Harvest while the head is firm and white and the spines have grown out. Our profile note is to harvest when the spines lengthen but before they yellow. The Minnesota DNR says lion's mane is best eaten white and that yellowing means aging and can taste bitter (Minnesota DNR). NCAT says the same: harvest lion's mane when the texture is firm and the shape is well developed (NCAT ATTRA 2026).

Cut it off at the base with a clean knife. Store it in the fridge at 34 to 38 °F (1 to 3 °C) in a paper bag or a vented container, not sealed plastic. NCAT gives most fresh mushrooms 5 to 7 days and says lion's mane can sometimes last a little longer (NCAT ATTRA 2026).

How to get a second flush

After the first harvest, clean off any bits left at the cut and let the block rest. NCAT suggests a rest of about 7 to 14 days between flushes, with the block kept damp (NCAT ATTRA 2026). Then set it up the same way. NCAT notes later flushes give diminishing returns, so expect a smaller second head.

If your lion's mane kit is not growing

Our profile expects knobs within the 5 day pinning stage. If there is nothing a week or so after that, it is usually one of these:

  • The air is too dry. Small dense blobs with no spines point here.
  • The room is too warm. Our profile fruits at 17 °C (63 °F), and NCAT puts lion's mane fruiting at 16 to 20 °C (60 to 68 °F).
  • It is sealed in a cupboard or bag with no fresh air. Fuzzy, misshapen growth points here.
  • It sits in the dark, or in bright light all day and night.
  • The cut dried out or was never made.

Mushroom grow kit not growing walks through each cause in order.

FAQ

How long does a lion's mane kit take to grow?

About 17 days from opening a colonized kit. Our profile gives 5 days of pinning and 12 days of fruiting before the end of the first harvest.

Should I mist my lion's mane kit?

Yes. Mist the air around the cut and inside a loose tent a few times a day, more in a dry room. Avoid soaking the spines or letting water pool at the cut.

Why is my lion's mane turning yellow?

It is aging, or the air around it is too dry or too drafty. Harvest it now. Next time pick sooner, and if the spines yellow early, cut back on fresh air and raise humidity a little.

Why is my lion's mane pink?

Usually stress, and it depends on the strain. A 2025 study got pink heads under nonstop 500 lux light at 17 to 18 °C and white heads at 200 lux or lower on a 12 hour cycle.

Does lion's mane need light to fruit?

A little. About 200 to 400 lux for 12 hours a day is enough. Room light or indirect daylight works.

Sources

  • Jozifek et al. 2025, Selenium Uptake by Hericium erinaceus Basidiocarps on Various Substrates and Their Effect on Growth and Yield, Agriculture 15(5):460
  • Niedzielski et al. 2014, Efficacy of supplementation of selected medicinal mushrooms with inorganic selenium salts, Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part B 49
  • Sokół et al. 2015, Biology, cultivation, and medicinal functions of the mushroom Hericium erinaceum, Acta Mycologica 50(2):1069
  • NCAT ATTRA 2026, Mushroom Cultivation, USDA funded grower publication IP677
  • Minnesota DNR, Minnesota Profile: Lion's Mane, Minnesota Conservation Volunteer 2018
  • Our lion's mane grow profile, for every stage length, temperature, humidity, light and fan setting above, and our pearl oyster and blue oyster profiles for the oyster fan comparison

item.title: How to fruit an oyster mushroom grow kit
item.description: An oyster kit fruits in about two weeks once it is cut open. Day by day steps for pearl and blue oysters, with humidity, fresh air, light and harvest timing.
item.content:encoded:
Cut the bag open on a fully white kit, keep the cut face damp but never dripping, give it plenty of fresh air and about 12 hours a day of low light, and keep it cool. Pins show in about 4 to 5 days and the first harvest is done about 13 to 15 days after you open it. Our pearl oyster profile pins at 18 °C (64 °F) and 93% humidity, then fruits at 16 °C (61 °F) and 88%. Blue oyster runs a few degrees cooler, at 15 °C (59 °F) to pin and 14 °C (57 °F) to fruit.

What an oyster kit needs to fruit

An oyster kit is a block of substrate that the mycelium has already grown through. The hard part is done when it arrives. Your job is to change four things so the block switches from growing mycelium to growing mushrooms: cooler air, damp air at the cut, fresh air, and light.

These are the settings in our free pearl oyster and blue oyster grow profiles. Pinning is when the tiny first mushrooms form. Fruiting is when they grow to picking size.

SettingPearl oysterBlue oyster
Pinning stage5 days4 days
Pinning temperature18 °C (64 °F)15 °C (59 °F)
Pinning humidity93%94%
Fruiting stage10 days9 days
Fruiting temperature16 °C (61 °F)14 °C (57 °F)
Fruiting humidity88%87%
Light, both stages12 h a day, about 90 lux, blue12 h a day, about 90 lux, blue
Chamber fan while fruiting40 s every 10 min40 s every 10 min

Pinning plus fruiting is 15 days for pearl and 13 days for blue. That is the count from a fully colonized kit to the end of the first harvest. Grower guides land in the same place: a USDA SARE funded oyster booklet puts the harvest about 5 to 10 days after a block goes into fruiting conditions (Crosby 2016).

Day by day steps for an oyster kit

  1. Day 0, check the block. It should be white and firm all the way through. Brown patches mean it is still colonizing, so keep it closed and warm for a few more days. Our profiles colonize at 24 °C (75 °F) for pearl and 22 °C (72 °F) for blue.
  2. Day 0, cut it open. Cut where the instructions that came with the kit say, usually an X or a slit in the side of the bag. Pins form where the block meets air, so that cut is where your mushrooms will grow.
  3. Day 0, move it somewhere cool and bright. Pick a spot around 15 to 18 °C (59 to 64 °F) with indirect daylight or room light, out of direct sun and away from heater vents.
  4. Days 1 to 5 (blue 1 to 4), keep the cut damp. Mist the cut face and the air around it once or twice a day, more in a dry heated room. Never let water pool on the block.
  5. Days 1 to 5 (blue 1 to 4), give it fresh air and light. Fresh air several times a day and about 12 hours of light a day tell the block it has reached open air. Pins usually show by day 4 or 5. Once they do, drop the room a couple of degrees if you can: 16 °C (61 °F) for pearl and 14 °C (57 °F) for blue.
  6. Days 6 to 15 (blue 5 to 13), let the clusters grow. Keep the air damp and give even more fresh air than before. Mist the air near the clusters, not the caps.
  7. By day 15 (blue day 13), harvest. Pick the whole cluster as the caps flatten out, before the edges flip up. Twist it off or cut it at the base.
  8. After the harvest, rest and repeat. Let the block rest, then set it up the same way for a second flush.

Plug your open date into the grow timeline calculator to get calendar dates for each stage.

Where to cut an oyster kit

Follow the kit's own instructions first, since some are built to fruit from a pre cut window or from the top. If there are none, one X or slit on the side facing the room works. Pins sometimes form inside the bag before you open it. If that happens, cut the bag right at that spot so they can reach air.

Should you mist an oyster kit?

Yes, but lightly, and the goal is damp air more than a wet block. A University of California grower guide runs oyster pinning at 95% humidity and mists once or twice a day until the mushrooms are 30 to 40% of harvest size. During cropping it runs 85 to 92% humidity and keeps misting to stop caps cracking (UC ANR).

Do not spray the caps hard. The SARE booklet warns that mushrooms soak up water they touch and turn soggy when sprayed over and over (Crosby 2016). Penn State lists a wet mushroom surface as one of the things that makes bacterial blotch worse (Royse, Penn State).

In a dry house, a loose plastic tent with a few holes over the kit holds humidity between mistings. Leave it loose so air still gets in.

How much fresh air does an oyster kit need?

A lot. The SARE booklet puts it simply: with oysters, the more fresh air the better. Mushrooms breathe out carbon dioxide, and too much of it gives long stems and small caps.

  • UC ANR runs 4 fresh air changes an hour at pinning and 4 to 6 while cropping, with carbon dioxide under 600 ppm (UC ANR).
  • Penn State brings in enough fresh air at pinning to drop carbon dioxide below 700 ppm (Royse, Penn State).
  • The SARE booklet aims for under 800 ppm and says fruiting can stall above 1200 ppm (Crosby 2016).

A kit on an open counter usually gets enough. A kit in a closed cupboard, a sealed bag or a small box does not. Our profiles step the fan up from pinning to fruiting for the same reason. If you grow in a box or chamber, check it with the fresh air planner, and see long stems and small caps if the clusters stretch.

How much light does an oyster kit need?

Not much. Penn State gives oysters 50 to 300 lux of cool white light after the spawn run (Royse, Penn State), and UC ANR says diffuse natural light is enough (UC ANR). Our profiles run 12 hours a day at about 90 lux with a blue bias, because oysters start fruiting under blue light and barely respond to red (Richartz and MacLellan 1987). Room light or a window with no direct sun does the job. Do mushrooms need light? has the full numbers.

What temperature should an oyster kit fruit at?

Cool room temperature. UC ANR pins oysters at 55 to 60 °F (13 to 16 °C) and crops them at 60 to 64 °F (16 to 18 °C) (UC ANR). The SARE booklet says most oysters fruit best in the mid 60s °F and keeps them between 55 and 70 °F (13 to 21 °C) (Crosby 2016). Penn State lists fruiting below 10 °C (50 °F) among the causes of deformed oysters (Royse, Penn State).

Blue oyster is the one to keep cool. In a warm room the blue fades toward grey and the stems get longer, which is why its profile fruits at 14 °C (57 °F). Pearl oyster is more forgiving and fruits at 16 °C (61 °F) in its profile.

When to harvest oyster mushrooms

Pick the whole cluster at once, when the caps are flattening out and the edges still have a slight roll. UC ANR harvests just before the curled cap edge turns flat (UC ANR). The SARE booklet says to pick before the edges flatten completely or flip up, which keeps the texture and cuts down on spores (Crosby 2016).

Do not wait long. Oysters grow fast, and the SARE booklet notes that in the 60s °F growers often pick twice a day. Mature oysters drop a lot of spores, and Penn State notes that inhaled spores can cause an allergic reaction in some people (Royse, Penn State). Another reason to pick on time and keep the kit somewhere with good airflow.

Store the harvest in the fridge in a paper bag or a container with holes. The SARE booklet keeps oysters at 36 to 38 °F (2 to 3 °C) for about 10 days, and says they rot in 1 to 2 days in a sealed container (Crosby 2016).

How to get a second flush

After the first harvest, pull off any stem bits left in the cut and let the block rest. UC ANR spaces oyster flushes about 10 days apart (UC ANR). A block that feels light and dry often pins again after a few hours soaking in cold water. Then set it up the same way as the first time. Each flush is usually smaller than the last.

If your oyster kit is not fruiting

Give it two weeks from the day you open it. If nothing has happened by then, the cause is almost always one of the same few things: the block was not fully colonized, the room is too warm, the cut dried out, there is too little fresh air, or it sits in a dark cupboard. Mushroom grow kit not growing walks through them in order, and why your mushrooms are not pinning covers fruiting triggers in more depth.

FAQ

How long does an oyster mushroom kit take to grow?

About two weeks from opening a fully colonized kit. Our profiles give 15 days for pearl oyster and 13 days for blue oyster from the first day of pinning to the end of the first harvest, with pins in 4 to 5 days.

Should I mist my oyster mushroom kit?

Yes, lightly. Mist the cut face and the air around it once or twice a day, more in a dry room, and never so much that water pools or runs off the caps.

Why are my oyster mushrooms all stem and no cap?

Too little fresh air. Carbon dioxide builds up around the kit and the stems stretch looking for open air. Move the kit out of any cupboard or sealed bag and give it more air.

Why did my blue oysters turn grey?

They were fruiting too warm. Blue oysters hold their color best below about 18 °C (64 °F), and our blue oyster profile fruits at 14 °C (57 °F).

When should I pick oyster mushrooms?

When the caps have mostly flattened but the edges still curl under a little. Pick the whole cluster at once, before the edges flip up.

Sources

  • UC ANR, Cultivating Mushrooms on Small Family Farms, oyster spawn run, pinning and cropping parameters
  • Royse, Cultivation of Oyster Mushrooms, Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences
  • Crosby 2016, Growing Oyster Mushrooms, USDA SARE funded grower booklet
  • Richartz and MacLellan 1987, Action spectra for hyphal aggregation in Pleurotus ostreatus, Photochemistry and Photobiology 45
  • Our pearl oyster and blue oyster grow profiles, for every stage length, temperature, humidity, light and fan setting above

item.title: Do mushrooms need light to grow?
item.description: Most mushrooms need light to fruit, but not much. Hours, lux and color for 20 species, with the study behind each number.
item.content:encoded:
Most mushrooms need some light to fruit, but not much and not for energy. Keep colonization dark, then give about 12 hours a day of low light once pins should form. About 50 to 500 lux of cool white or blue light is enough for oysters, lion's mane, maitake and reishi. Button mushrooms need none, and enoki grown dark makes long white stems.

Why do mushrooms need light if they do not photosynthesize?

Mushrooms get their energy from the substrate, not from light. Light is a signal. For many species it tells the mycelium it has reached open air, which is where a mushroom should grow. A 2018 review of fruiting triggers lists light as a fruiting cue for many mushroom forming fungi, with blue light as the usual signal (Sakamoto 2018).

That is why the amount needed is small. You are not feeding the mushroom. You are telling it which way is up and that it is time to fruit.

How much light do mushrooms need?

Less than most people think. These are the numbers that show up in published work:

  • Oysters: Penn State's oyster production guide says the spawn run can go without light. After it, 50 to 300 lux of cool white light is enough (Royse, Penn State).
  • Lion's mane: white fruit bodies at 200 lux on a 12 hour cycle. The same study ran 500 lux for 24 hours a day and got pink stress coloring (Jozifek et al. 2025).
  • Maitake: primordia formed best at 200 lux and yield was best at 500 lux (Chi et al. 2008).
  • Reishi: 200 to 500 lux early in fruiting and 500 to 1000 lux later, from a literature table in a reishi cultivation thesis (Maszlaver 2011).
  • Cordyceps militaris: the brightest of the group. Highest dry yield at about 1750 lux and highest cordycepin at about 1250 lux, on 12 hours a day (Wu et al. 2016).

A free phone light meter app gives a rough lux reading at the spot where your block sits. That is close enough for these ranges.

How many hours of light a day?

12 hours on and 12 hours off is the schedule used in most of the studies above and in every lit stage of our profiles. More is not better. The lion's mane study above is the clearest example: 24 hours of light at 500 lux stressed the fruit bodies pink, and 12 hours at 200 lux did not.

A plug-in outlet timer is all you need to hold that schedule.

Does the color of light matter?

Yes. Blue does the signaling for most species, and red does very little.

  • In oyster mushrooms, the first step of fruiting responds most to light at 370 nm and 440 to 450 nm, and wavelengths longer than 530 nm gave no response (Richartz and MacLellan 1987).
  • Blue LED light at 430 to 470 nm improved oyster cap growth and red light did not (Wang et al. 2020). A 2024 trial found the same for cap size at 450 nm against 610 nm (De Bonis et al. 2024).
  • Blue light also triggered king oyster primordia to turn into fruit bodies (Xie et al. 2018).
  • Maitake is the exception. White light outyielded blue and green in the 2008 trial, so our maitake profile uses white only (Chi et al. 2008).

In practice, a cool white LED (5000 to 6500 K) has plenty of blue in it. You do not need a special grow light. A red or warm 2700 K bulb is the one choice to avoid.

Light for each species we grow

This is what each of our 20 free culinary grow profiles runs. Every lit stage is 12 hours a day. Where no study gave a number for that species, the profile uses a labeled low light default of about 90 lux with a blue bias, inside the Penn State 50 to 300 lux range.

Which mushrooms grow without light?

Two common ones.

  • Button and cremini (Agaricus bisporus) do not need light to fruit. Their triggers are temperature, carbon dioxide, the casing layer and volatiles (Baars et al. 2020). Penn State's Agaricus guide grows them without light too (Penn State Extension).
  • Enoki (Flammulina velutipes) fruits in the dark after a temperature drop, and the dark fruit bodies are long, pale and pinhead sized. Light is what forms a proper cap (Sakamoto 2004). The thin white enoki in stores are grown this way on purpose.

Should mycelium be kept dark while it colonizes?

Yes, or close to it. Every one of our profiles runs colonization dark. Penn State's oyster guide runs the spawn run without artificial light. Since light is a fruiting cue, light during colonization can start pins early, which is why our lion's mane profile keeps that stage dark.

Shiitake is the one to watch. After colonization the block needs a lit rest to brown its skin, since that brown coat is light induced (Yoo et al. 2019). Our shiitake profile browns the block under 12 hours a day at about 200 lux, based on the work reviewed in a 2024 blue light study (Kim et al. 2024). Light is also needed for normal shiitake fruiting (Leatham and Stahmann 1987).

Signs your mushrooms need more or less light

  • No pins on a fully colonized block: light may be missing, but check fresh air and humidity first. Our not pinning guide walks through the order.
  • Long stems with small caps: usually too much carbon dioxide, and sometimes too little light. See long stems and small caps.
  • Pale maitake: maitake grown in the dark kept pale caps (Kurahashi et al. 2015).
  • Lion's mane turning pink: the 2025 study above got pink coloring from 24 hour light at 500 lux. Try a 12 hour window at lower light.

FAQ

Can mushrooms grow in complete darkness?

Button, cremini and enoki can. Most other species will try to fruit in the dark but make pale, stretched or misshapen mushrooms, because light is the cue that shapes the cap.

Is sunlight good for mushrooms?

Indirect daylight is fine for most species. Direct sun is not, because it heats and dries the block fast.

Do mushrooms need a grow light?

No. Any cool white LED or a bright room is enough for most species. A dedicated light helps only in a closed box or closet with no other light, and then a small LED strip on a timer does the job.

What color light is best for mushrooms?

Blue or cool white. Studies on oysters and king oysters found blue light drives fruiting and red light does little. Maitake did best under white.
